issues.legal_issue: A strong presumption of joint status among Hindu brothers is not displaced by a mutation entry alone, and the party alleging severance must establish it.
material_facts: The two claimants and their deceased brother were brothers and were found to have constituted a joint Hindu family.
The respondent alleged that the deceased brother had separated from his brothers, but did not establish when the alleged severance occurred.
The mutation in the respondent’s favour followed her husband’s death while the claimants were minors; the record did not show that they or their guardian had notice or objected after being heard.
The revenue entries and other conduct relied on to prove severance were explained or did not reliably establish separation; the oral evidence for separation was found insufficient.
The Court found that the evidence established that the deceased brother died as a member of the joint Hindu family.
issues.conclusion: The joint Hindu family had not been proved to have been severed, and the deceased brother died as a member of it; the mutation entry in the widow’s favour did not establish otherwise.
issues.legal_principle: There is a strong presumption in favour of Hindu brothers constituting a joint family, and the person alleging severance bears the burden of establishing it. A mutation entry made in favour of a widow after her husband’s death, without more, is not a clear indication that the family had been severed. No earlier case was relied on for this principle.

rule.if: joint_family_property_appeal and brothers_in_joint_family and severance_claimed and (mutation_lacked_notice or severance_evidence_weak)

predicates.joint_family_property_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a claim to property on the basis of joint Hindu family status.
predicates.brothers_in_joint_family: The persons whose joint status is disputed are Hindu brothers who constituted a joint family.
predicates.severance_claimed: A party asserted that one brother had separated from the joint family.
predicates.mutation_lacked_notice: A revenue mutation was made without notice to, or an opportunity to object by, the affected family members or their representative.
predicates.severance_evidence_weak: The evidence relied on to establish separation did not reliably prove that severance had occurred.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns property claimed through a joint family of Hindu brothers and the asserted severance is not reliably established, the joint family is treated as continuing at the relevant death.

issues.legal_issue: A party’s duly proved and clear admissions are substantive evidence even if the party is not confronted with them while testifying.
material_facts: The respondent made statements in documents describing the family or firm as joint, including statements in pleadings and an agreement concerning arbitration.
Evidence was given to prove those documents and the respondent’s connection to their contents.
The respondent was not confronted with the admissions when she entered the witness box.
The respondent’s statement that her husband had separated from his brothers before her marriage did not adequately explain or clearly deny the facts admitted.
issues.conclusion: The duly proved admissions could be used as evidence against the respondent despite her not having been confronted with them while testifying.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 17 and 21 of the Indian Evidence Act, admissions are substantive evidence of the facts admitted, although they are not conclusive proof. Section 145 serves the different purpose of contradicting a witness; a prior statement used for contradiction does not thereby become substantive evidence. The Court discussed Firm Malik Des Rai v. Firm Piara Lal, Ayodhya Prasad v. Bhawani Shanker, and Bal Gangadhar Tilak v. Shrinivas Pandit, and held that the latter did not directly decide the admissibility of duly proved admissions not put to their maker in testimony. Admissions must be clear to be used against their maker, and their weight is distinct from their admissibility.

predicates.party_admission_evidence_dispute: The proceeding involves whether a party’s prior statement may be used as an admission.
predicates.admission_duly_proved: Evidence establishes that the party made the prior statement.
predicates.admission_clear: The statement clearly supports the fact for which it is relied on.

issues.definition: When a party’s clear prior admission is duly proved in an admission-evidence dispute, it is admissible as substantive evidence.

issues.legal_issue: A property-title suit is not time-barred where the defendant did not previously assert an adverse title or act to oust the claimants and the suit followed the later assertion of adverse rights.
material_facts: The respondent’s claim that she owned the property from the time of her husband’s death was not supported by good evidence of an earlier adverse assertion or ouster.
The dispute between the parties arose years before the respondent began leasing or transferring properties in a manner asserting her title.
The claimants filed suit soon after those acts asserting title.
issues.conclusion: The suit was not barred by limitation.
issues.legal_principle: The Court found no basis to treat the respondent as having asserted an adverse right or ousted the claimants before the dispute arose, and held that the suit brought soon after her later acts asserting title was within time. The Court cited no provision or earlier case for this conclusion.

predicates.property_title_declaration_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking a declaration of rights to property.
predicates.no_earlier_adverse_assertion: The defendant did not previously assert a right adverse to the claimants or act to exclude them from the property.
predicates.suit_filed_soon_after_adverse_act: The claimants filed suit soon after the defendant began acts asserting an adverse title.

issues.definition: A property-title declaration suit is not time-barred where there was no earlier adverse assertion and suit followed soon after the defendant’s adverse act.
